title: What is a Power Dialer? Pros, Cons & Alternatives
summary: Struggling to understand the concept of a power dialer, auto dialing software and how to use such tech? Here's what you need to know.
body_text: Up until recently, most sales teams were at the mercy of their dialer - manually clicking through prospects and accounts one at a time. Even with the most high-tech dialers, the manual workflow of clicking and typing out call notes boggs down the user experience and takes your focus away from what really matters… Having more conversations! But now we have access to hundreds of AI automations to take this burden off our backs, one of them being a power dialer. To enable your business we’ll be talking about different types of dialing technology & showcase how Trellus can help you make the best choice for your call center or business. So, What is a Power Dialer? Power dialers are sophisticated telecommunications systems that streamline outbound calling operations through automated processes and intelligent workflow management. At their core, these systems operate by automatically initiating calls from a predetermined list of contacts, eliminating the need for manual dialing while ensuring regulatory compliance. The fundamental workflow begins when the system loads a contact list, typically integrated with a CRM platform . As an agent becomes available, the power dialer automatically initiates the next call in the queue, detecting busy signals, voicemails, or no-answers without agent intervention. Upon successful connection, the system immediately displays relevant contact information and call scripts to the agent. Key technical features include: Voicemail detection and automated drop Click-to-call functionality for manual override Real-time call analytics and monitoring Automated call recording and transcription CRM synchronization for contact updates The integration with CRM systems is particularly crucial, allowing for bidirectional data flow. As sales teams look toward the future, the role of automation continues to expand. Exploring the capabilities of power dialers in 2026 reveals how these tools are evolving to offer even more seamless CRM integrations and intelligent workflow features. When a call connects, the system automatically logs the interaction, updates contact status, and records call outcomes. This integration enables detailed tracking of campaign performance and individual agent productivity. Modern power dialers also incorporate regulatory compliance features, automatically adhering to calling hours restrictions, maintaining do-not-call lists, and recording consent management. Advanced systems can adjust dialing rates based on agent availability and campaign parameters, optimizing the balance between call volume and quality of interaction. How Does a Power Dialer Work? Now that we have a better understanding of what a Power Dialer is all about, let's discuss what it entails at a practical level. ‍ As soon as the agent completes a call, the system will dial the next phone number on auto from the contact list. This enables the call agent and there is a limited learning curve in terms of how it functions since it’s all automated. ‍ By focusing on automated workflows and tools, here’s what power dialing could do for your sales team: Control Call Pacing: Calls are made in a steady manner which ensures all call regulations and maintains call quality. Enhanced Time Efficiency: By automating the dialing process, agents are spared the need to manually handle unproductive outcomes such as answering machines, busy lines, or disconnected numbers, resulting in significant time savings. Reduced Burnout: Removing repetitive admin work allows reps to serve clients more efficiently—leading to less stress and more satisfaction. Instant Response: Agents hear the recipient the moment the call connects—allowing them to respond instantly, without delays or awkward pauses. Seamless Scalability & Collaboration: Empower your call center teams to expand globally and handle higher volumes—without adding to their workload or compromising teamwork. Power Dialer vs Predictive Dialer - What's The Difference? Power dialers operate on a one-to-one ratio, initiating the next call only when an agent becomes available, ensuring more personalized customer interactions and greater agent control over the calling process. Key differences between the systems: Power dialers maintain consistent agent availability Predictive dialers use algorithms to anticipate availability Power dialers offer higher personalization potential Predictive dialers excel in high-volume scenarios Power dialers minimize abandoned calls Predictive dialers, on the other hand, employ sophisticated algorithms to forecast agent availability and dial multiple numbers simultaneously, anticipating when agents will complete their current calls. While this approach maximizes efficiency in high-volume environments, it can result in longer pause times and higher abandon rates when connections are made before agents are ready. Power dialers, however, prioritize call quality and personalization over pure volume. They give agents more control over their calling pace and ensure immediate availability when connections are made. Pros and Cons of Power Dialers Power dialers offer significant advantages for outbound calling operations while also presenting certain limitations that businesses must carefully consider. Understanding these pros and cons is crucial for organizations evaluating their communications technology needs. Key advantages of power dialers include: Elimination of manual dialing errors Increased agent productivity Automated compliance management Enhanced lead management Improved contact rates The primary benefits stem from automation, which significantly reduces manual tasks and human error while increasing overall efficiency. Organizations must also consider challenges like sales call delays during high-volume periods and the need for consistent internet connectivity. While voicemail assistants and automated features streamline operations, they may sometimes impact the personal touch in customer interactions. What Other Aspects of Auto Dialing & Power Dialer Software Do You Need To Know? Sales teams are always looking for ways to enhance efficiency, maximize productivity, and drive revenue. One of the tools gaining popularity in the sales landscape is the power dialer . While we kicked things off with some of the basic concepts of power dialers and how they work and all, there are tons of things that haven’t been touched upon. To fully appreciate the depth of power dialer software and its impact on modern sales operations , we need to explore its extended functionalities, advanced use cases, and how it integrates with other sales techs. We'll look at several advanced angles and factors that differentiate the best power dialer solutions , the nuances of a single-line dialer , and options like a free power dialer for small businesses or startups. The Difference Between Power Dialers and Other ‘Traditional’ Dialing Systems While it’s already been established that power dialers automate the dialing process by calling one contact after another, it's important to differentiate power dialers from other systems like predictive dialers, progressive dialers, and parallel dialers. When evaluating the best fit for your sales team, understanding the nuances of a power dialer vs parallel dialer is crucial. While both automate outreach, choosing between them depends heavily on whether your strategy prioritizes sheer volume or conversational quality. And yes, if you’re in an auto dialer vs. power dialer predicament, both are the same thing IF the baseline features and capabilities of the programs are similar. Predictive dialers focus on initiating calls based on the availability of agents, often dialing multiple numbers at once. These systems predict when an agent will become available and dial ahead of time, but this can result in abandoned calls if prospects pick up before agents are ready. Progressive dialers automate calling but don’t dial the next number until the agent finishes the current call. In other words, it’s similar to power dialing, but the distinction is that progressive dialers are more passive in their approach and are ideal for low-volume calling environments. Parallel dialers allow multiple numbers to be dialed simultaneously and connect the agent to whichever call is answered first. In contrast, your typical modern-day power dialers maintain a one-at-a-time workflow, ensuring no contact is wasted or dropped. This clear distinction shows that power dialer software is often the go-to option for teams looking for a balance between automation and control. The single-line dialer feature makes it ideal for high-quality conversations where each lead receives full attention without any disconnects or dropped calls. Advanced Use Cases for Power Dialers Beyond just improving dialing efficiency, power dialers offer advanced features that cater to more specific sales strategies. Here are a few notable use cases that may not have been previously discussed: Outbound Sales at Scale Power dialers are exceptionally well-suited for outbound sales campaigns where reps need to call large volumes of prospects. However, these campaigns can be tailored to different sales approaches: Cold Calling : A power dialer can help SDRs (Sales Development Representatives) call through large lists of leads without the distraction of manual dialing. Warm Leads : Power dialers also shine in scenarios where a list of warm leads has been generated through marketing campaigns or previous interactions. In these cases, the conversation is often more in-depth, and the streamlined workflow enables reps to take detailed notes or follow up immediately. Customer Retention and Upselling For teams focused on customer success, power dialers can be a great asset for managing customer outreach. Whether it’s renewing subscriptions, conducting satisfaction surveys, or offering upsell opportunities, power dialers help maintain consistent and structured communication with existing clients. Automating post-call workflows, including note-taking and call disposition, allows agents to spend more time building meaningful relationships with customers. Follow-up Campaigns Following up with leads who have shown some interest but haven’t yet converted is a critical part of sales . Power dialers enable reps to schedule follow-up calls and automate reminders for more systematic outreach. With built-in CRM integration, sales reps don’t need to manually sift through notes—they are prompted when follow-ups are due, making sure no lead is forgotten. Multi-location or Distributed Teams If your sales team is spread across multiple locations or works remotely, a power dialer software solution can create a unified workflow. Every sales rep can have access to the same dialer functionality, and the system can coordinate outreach across different time zones seamlessly. The integration with cloud-based CRMs ensures all customer data is updated in real time, keeping everyone aligned. Power Dialer vs Predictive Dialer The comparison between a Power Dialer vs Predictive Dialer comes down to dialing strategy. A power dialer calls one lead at a time, automatically moving to the next after completing or skipping a call, ensuring focused, quality interactions. In contrast, a predictive dialer uses algorithms to call multiple numbers simultaneously, predicting agent availability to minimize downtime and maximize call volume. Power dialers are ideal for personalized outreach, while predictive dialers suit large-scale campaigns where efficiency is key. The choice depends on whether your priority is meaningful engagement or high-volume lead generation. Power Dialer vs Parallel Dialer The difference between a Power Dialer vs Parallel Dialer lies in their dialing methods. A power dialer calls one contact at a time, ensuring focused and personalized interactions, making it ideal for quality-driven outreach. On the other hand, a parallel dialer dials multiple numbers simultaneously, connecting agents to the first person who answers, prioritizing speed and efficiency. Power dialers are suited for teams emphasizing meaningful conversations, while parallel dialers are best for high-volume calling campaigns. Choosing between them depends on your sales strategy and the balance between quality and quantity in your outreach efforts. Benefits and Use Cases of Power Dialers Power dialers have revolutionized outbound calling campaigns by dramatically improving efficiency and productivity in various business settings. These systems eliminate manual dialing, allowing sales teams and customer service representatives to focus on meaningful conversations rather than administrative tasks. Essential benefits that drive adoption: Increased daily call volume (typically 2-3x improvement) Enhanced contact rates through local presence dialing Real-time performance analytics Seamless CRM integration The technology's integration with CRM systems creates a streamlined workflow where agents have instant access to relevant contact information and can track sales productivity metrics to improve performance. This ensures that when a connection is made, the agent is fully prepared with contextual information, leading to more personalized and effective conversations. Power dialers help maintain compliance with regulations such as TCPA and DNC lists through automated screening and record-keeping. These systems can automatically adjust calling times based on time zones and maintain detailed logs of all calling activity, providing essential documentation for regulatory requirements. Key Metrics and Reporting in Power Dialers The AI-generated analytics that we talked about earlier offer a good starting point, but it’s important to note the breadth of reporting capabilities available in the best power dialer platforms. Sales leaders today need data-driven insights to make informed decisions, and power dialers go beyond basic call logs. Here are a few essential metrics: Call Connect Rates : Power dialers can track how many calls actually connect with prospects versus how many result in voicemail or no answer. This data helps sales teams understand which times of day are most effective for calling and adjust strategies accordingly. Average Call Duration : While talking more may sound positive, power dialers help analyze if longer calls are driving results or simply wasting time. Understanding the ideal call length can optimize the balance between time spent and conversions. Conversion Rate per Call : For each call made through a power dialer, sales teams can track whether it leads to the desired outcome (i.e., booking a meeting, closing a deal, etc.). This allows for a better understanding of which sales tactics work best during the call. Agent Performance : Power dialer systems can monitor individual agent performance, identifying which team members are closing the most deals or having the most productive conversations. Sales managers can use this data to offer coaching or redistribute leads for optimal efficiency. The Role of CRM Integration in Power Dialers One of the biggest advantages of modern power dialer software is its ability to seamlessly integrate with CRM systems. This integration ensures that every interaction with a lead or customer is automatically logged into the CRM, making it easier to track the entire customer journey. More importantly, it allows for: Automatic Contact Updates : Any changes made during a call—such as adding new notes, updating contact information, or changing deal status—are instantly synced with the CRM, eliminating manual data entry. Task Automation : After each call, tasks can be automatically generated, such as scheduling follow-up meetings or sending additional materials to the prospect. This reduces administrative workload and ensures next steps are always clear. Enhanced Personalization : With all the customer information readily available in the CRM, power dialers enable sales reps to personalize their calls. The integration pulls data points like recent activity, previous conversations, and purchase history, allowing reps to tailor their pitch in real time. title: GSK’s investigational liver therapy, efimosfermin, receives US FDA Breakthrough Therapy and EMA Priority Medicines (PRIME) designations for MASH
summary: Designations recognise potential for efimosfermin to address significant unmet medical need & reflect momentum in GSKs liver health pipeline
body_text: 27 April 2026 Issued: London, UK For media and investors only GSK’s investigational liver therapy, efimosfermin, receives US FDA Breakthrough Therapy and EMA Priority Medicines (PRIME) designations for MASH Download (PDF - 189.3KB) Phase II data show once-monthly efimosfermin improved liver fibrosis (scarring), a key driver of disease progression in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) MASH is a leading cause of liver transplant in the US and Europe Designations recognise potential for efimosfermin to address significant unmet medical need and reflect momentum in GSK’s liver health pipeline GSK plc (LSE/NYSE: GSK) today announced that efimosfermin, a once-monthly investigational liver therapy, has been granted Breakthrough Therapy Designation by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and Priority Medicines (PRIME) Designation by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for the treatment of MASH. The FDA designation is designed to expedite the development and review of medicines for serious conditions, where preliminary clinical evidence indicates the potential for substantial improvement over available therapy.1 The EMA designation provides scientific and regulatory support for medicines that have the potential to address significant unmet medical need.2 Kaivan Khavandi, SVP, R&D Head Respiratory, Immunology & Inflammation (RI&I), and Head of Translational & Development Sciences, GSK , said: “MASH affects millions of people worldwide and is one of the leading causes of liver transplant in the US and Europe, but treatment options are limited for most and non-existent for those with the most advanced form of disease. These designations recognise efimosfermin’s potential and reflect GSK’s accelerating momentum in liver health. We believe efimosfermin has the potential to significantly advance the standard of care by directly targeting liver fibrosis.” The two designations were supported by data from MASH patients with moderate to advanced (F2/F3) and cirrhotic (F4) fibrosis. This includes phase II data at 48 weeks for F2/F3 patients who showed fibrosis improvement and MASH resolution with once-monthly efimosfermin versus placebo. Data also confirmed a well-tolerated safety profile with mild, transient adverse events, including nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea.3,4 Efimosfermin is currently in phase III with the ZENITH-1 and ZENITH-2 trials investigating efficacy and safety in MASH patients with F2/F3 fibrosis. Phase III trials in MASH patients with F4 fibrosis are expected to start this year. MASH is a chronic, progressive liver disease that affects up to 5% of the global population and is a leading cause of liver transplants in both the US and Europe.5-7 The buildup of scar tissue, or fibrosis, is a key predictor of serious outcomes for patients, including cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer.8 Currently, liver-specific treatment options are limited for those with moderate to advanced fibrosis and there are no approved treatments for cirrhotic MASH (F4).8 About efimosfermin Efimosfermin is an investigational, once-monthly subcutaneous injection of a long-acting variant of FGF21 that is designed to regulate key metabolic pathways to decrease liver fat, ameliorate liver inflammation, and reverse liver fibrosis in patients with MASH. Efimosfermin is currently in trials for moderate to advanced fibrosis, including cirrhosis, and is not available for prescription anywhere in the world. About GSK research in hepatology GSK is extending its expertise in inflammation to develop a next wave of innovation for the millions of people affected by chronic and life-threatening fibro-inflammatory liver conditions. Harnessing the science of the immune system and advanced technologies, GSK is committed to advancing its hepatology pipeline with potential therapies for chronic hepatitis B, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD). title: Property Management KPIs That Actually Drive Decisions
summary: The five KPIs every multifamily operator tracks and the three most miss because their data does not support them.
body_text: Apr 8, 2026 · Propexo Team Property Management KPIs That Actually Drive Decisions Every multifamily operator has a dashboard. Most of them show the same five numbers: occupancy, rent, collections, work orders, and turnover. These are table stakes. You need them, but they are not what separates a top-quartile portfolio from an average one. The difference comes down to three property management KPIs that most operators cannot track accurately — not because they do not know about them, but because their data infrastructure does not support them. The property management system (PMS) was never designed to be an analytics platform. And when you are running three PMS platforms across a portfolio assembled through acquisitions, the gap between what you want to measure and what you can actually measure gets wide. This post covers both sides. The five standard property management KPIs you should already be tracking, and the three that require a different approach to data before they become useful. The Five KPIs Every Operator Tracks These are not optional. If you are a VP of Operations reporting to a COO or a board, these numbers come up in every meeting. The question is not whether you track them — it is whether you trust them. Occupancy Rate Occupancy rate is the most visible metric in multifamily property management. It is calculated as total occupied units divided by total available units, expressed as a percentage. Most operators track this at the portfolio level and break it down by property. That is necessary but not sufficient. The number that matters more is occupancy by unit type — one-beds versus two-beds versus three-beds — because it tells you where demand is shifting before portfolio-level occupancy moves. Data source: PMS lease records, unit inventory. The challenge runs deeper than system fragmentation. Your internal occupancy definition will often differ from what your PMS calculates out of the box. You might count a unit as occupied on lease execution, while your PMS counts it as occupied on move-in. You might exclude corporate housing or short-term leases from occupancy, while the PMS includes them. Reconciling these definitional differences across properties requires both standardized logic and consistent application at every site. If you run two PMS platforms, occupancy data lives in two systems with different unit-type taxonomies and different occupancy logic. Reconciling them manually in a spreadsheet works for a quarterly board deck. It does not work for weekly operating decisions. Effective Rent Growth Effective rent growth measures what tenants actually pay after concessions, free months, and lease incentives are factored in. It is distinct from asking rent and market rent. Tracking effective rent growth versus market comps tells you whether your pricing strategy is working or whether you are buying occupancy with concessions. The number is useless in isolation. It needs to be compared against submarket benchmarks on a rolling basis. Data source: PMS lease records (rent rolls, concession tracking), third-party market data from providers such as CoStar or Yardi Matrix. This one breaks down fast when concessions are tracked inconsistently across properties. One regional manager enters a free month as a concession. Another adjusts the base rent. Your effective rent calculation is wrong before it reaches the dashboard. Maintenance Cost Per Unit Maintenance cost per unit is calculated as total maintenance spend divided by total units. Simple in concept. Hard to get right in practice. The useful version of this metric is not the portfolio average. It is the property-level breakdown by maintenance category — appliance, plumbing, HVAC, common area — compared against property age and unit count. That breakdown tells you which properties are trending toward capital expenditure problems and which are operating efficiently. Data source: PMS work order systems, accounts payable, vendor invoicing. The problem: maintenance data is the messiest data in property management. Work orders live in the PMS. Vendor invoices live in the accounting system. Matching them requires a common identifier that often does not exist, especially when maintenance is handled by a mix of in-house staff and third-party vendors. Time-to-Lease Time-to-lease is the number of days from when a unit becomes available (move-out or notice-to-vacate) to a signed lease. Not move-in — signed lease. Time-to-lease is a leading indicator for occupancy. If it is trending up, occupancy will drop in 30 to 60 days. If it is trending down, your leasing team and pricing strategy are working. Tracking it by property and by unit type gives you early signal on where to allocate marketing spend and where to adjust rents. Data source: PMS lease records (notice dates, vacancy dates, application dates, lease execution dates). This metric requires four date fields to calculate correctly. Most PMS platforms automatically capture notice-to-vacate dates and lease execution dates with accuracy because these trigger system workflows and compliance requirements. Application dates and lease execution dates flow reliably through the system as part of the lease workflow. The dates that break down are vacancy dates and lease execution dates that depend on whether the site team logs data consistently. One property that does not record when a unit physically became available or that leaves lease execution dates blank throws off the portfolio average. Worse, if different properties enter these dates at different points in their process — some on offer, some on application, some on actual execution — your portfolio-level time-to-lease becomes directionally useless. Resident Retention Rate Resident retention rate is the percentage of residents who renew their lease at expiration rather than moving out. Retention is cheaper than turnover — every operator knows this. Fewer operators measure it accurately. The real retention metric is not the binary renew-or-leave number. It is retention segmented by lease term, unit type, and tenure. A resident who has been in place for three years and renews at a 5% increase is a very different signal than a first-year resident who renews at flat rent. Data source: PMS lease records (lease start, expiration, renewal, and move-out dates). Retention data is usually clean within a single PMS. The problem is aggregating it across platforms and comparing it against the concessions you offered to get those renewals. Without that context, a high retention rate might be masking a rent-growth problem. The Three Property Management KPIs Most Operators Miss These are not obscure metrics. Most operators know they matter. The issue is that tracking them accurately requires data that does not live in one place — and often does not exist in a structured format at all. Revenue Per Available Unit (RevPAU) Revenue Per Available Unit (RevPAU) is a metric borrowed from hospitality and adapted for multifamily. RevPAU combines occupancy, rental income, and ancillary revenue (parking, pet fees, storage, amenity fees) into a single number that reflects how well you are monetizing your physical asset. RevPAU = Total Revenue / Total Available Units RevPAU is more useful than occupancy or effective rent alone because it captures the full revenue picture. A property at 93% occupancy with strong ancillary revenue can outperform a property at 97% occupancy that leaves money on the table. Why most operators cannot track it: Ancillary revenue is often tracked in the accounting system but not tied to individual units or unit types in the PMS. Parking revenue might be a line item in the general ledger with no connection to which units those tenants occupy. Pet fees might be tracked in a separate spreadsheet. Pulling all of these into a single per-unit calculation requires data normalization that most property management reporting setups do not support. What it requires: A unified data layer that maps revenue streams from both the PMS and the accounting system to individual units. Not a manual spreadsheet. An automated pipeline that updates as transactions post. Lease Conversion Efficiency Lease conversion efficiency is the ratio of signed leases to total qualified leads or tours. Not just leads — qualified leads. And not just applications — signed leases. This metric tells you how effective your leasing operation is at converting demand into revenue. A property with high traffic but low conversion has a different problem than a property with low traffic and high conversion. They need different interventions. Without this metric, both properties look the same until occupancy drops. Why most operators cannot track it: Lead and tour data lives in the CRM or lead management system — platforms such as Knock, Funnel Leasing, or RentCafe. Lease execution data lives in the PMS. Connecting the two requires matching prospects in the CRM to leases in the PMS — often across different identifiers with no shared key. Many operators calculate a rough version of this metric by dividing total leases by total leads. That number is directionally useful but masks the conversion funnel. You need stage-by-stage visibility: inquiry to tour, tour to application, application to lease. Each stage requires a different data source. What it requires: Integration between your CRM and PMS with identity resolution — matching the person in one system to the same person in the other. Plus consistent data entry standards across every site team. Controllable Expense Ratio Controllable expense ratio is total controllable operating expenses (payroll, maintenance, marketing, utilities where sub-metered, vendor contracts) divided by effective gross income. This is the metric that tells you whether your operational execution is improving or whether rising rents are covering up operational bloat. NOI growth gets the attention. But NOI can grow while your operations get less efficient if rents are rising fast enough. The controllable expense ratio strips out capital expenditures and fixed costs to show you how well you are managing the things you can actually manage. Why most operators cannot track it: Controllable versus non-controllable expense classification requires a standardized chart of accounts across every entity and property. After an acquisition, the acquired portfolio often runs on a different chart of accounts. Reconciling them is a months-long accounting project. Until it is done, portfolio-level controllable expense ratios are unreliable. What it requires: A normalized chart of accounts across all entities, mapped at a granular enough level to separate controllable from non-controllable expenses. Plus automated data feeds from every accounting system in the portfolio. The Infrastructure Problem Behind Property Management KPIs A pattern runs through every KPI on this list. The metric itself is not complicated. The math is straightforward. The difficulty is getting clean, timely, normalized data from systems that were never designed to talk to each other. Most operators solve this with spreadsheets and analyst headcount. A reporting analyst pulls data from three PMS platforms, normalizes it in Excel, and produces a weekly report. That works until it does not — until the analyst leaves, or the portfolio grows, or the board wants daily data instead of weekly. The operators who track all eight of these property management KPIs in real time have invested in a data infrastructure layer that sits between their source systems and their reporting tools. That layer handles normalization, identity resolution, and automated updates. It turns fragmented PMS data into a single source of truth that feeds a reliable property management dashboard. That infrastructure is not optional if you want to compete on operational execution. It is the difference between managing by intuition and managing by signal. What to Do Next If you are tracking the first five property management KPIs and getting useful answers, you are in good shape. The next step is honest assessment: can your current data infrastructure support the other three? If the answer is no, the fix is not a better dashboard. It is a better data layer. Start by auditing where each data point lives, how often it updates, and what it takes to normalize it across your portfolio. That audit will tell you exactly where the gaps are and what it will cost to close them. The KPIs themselves are not the hard part. Getting the data right is.
